What was required was a balanced assessment of the achievements of the period, across a range of examples, with specific support. The students were secure on the Dawes Plan, the Kellogg-Briand Pact, and the League of Nations. There was quite good knowledge of Locarno and some awareness of the Treaty of Mutual Assistance and the Geneva Protocol. Reference to events outside the given years could only be credited only as far as they were used to enhance the argument offered about 1923-1928.
70422k-jun24-01-q:
With this question, students were required to evaluate the value of three separate sources in relation to an issue –the escalation of the Second World War in 1941. They were not asked to compare the given sources and those who did wasted valuable time, although they were not penalised for so doing. The answer did not require an introduction or an overall conclusion, but some concluding judgement on each source in relation to the question posed was helpful to meet the criteria for the highest marks. The best answers were a nuanced evaluation of both provenance and content of the sources. Formulaic, rote- learned approaches were often less effective. A significant number of students were able to identify features about provenance (eg that Source A was said by Molotov who was involved in the signing of the Nazi-Soviet Pact) but then were not able to evaluate this beyond a simple comment that ‘they were there at the time and so this source is accurate’. This approach often leads to much speculation around provenance (for example assuming that Kleist was anti communist) which is not then borne out by the content of the source. The best answers were able to combine the two. A good example of this might be an answer to Source B which argued that the context of Tojo writing the diary in prison as a justification of his actions at the time of the strike on Pearl Harbour. This possible limitation is then borne out within the content of the source which is rather vague and even says ‘Japan lost all hope…’. Here, the student has suggested a limitation, but then was able to back it up by connecting provenance comments to the content of the source. This is a very effective technique which leads to high marks. Simply identifying provenance and making a vague assertion about tone does not lead to higher marks. The sources were mostly understood, but a surprising number of students thought that the British Journalist wrote Source C, which did affect how convincing their analysis was. Some students knew some interesting contextual details about the sources, especially Molotov and Tojo, and were able to deploy this knowledge to produce very effective analyses. It was disappointing to see a persistent minority making very few references to ‘value’ at all and conflating this with validity, utility, reliability and accuracy, which are not the same thing. Unfortunately, some students seemed to forget the question they were being asked to answer and started debating whether 1941 was when the USA got involved in the war, writing at length on issues such as Lend-Lease but this was not the question being asked. Similarly, for Source A there were some students who made extensive comments on Stalin’s Five Year Plans as a prelude to war and again this was not required for this question. It is vital that regular links to the wording of the specific question are made in order to maintain focus and support any evaluations with contextual knowledge.

There were still a number of students paraphrasing the sources and offering very little if any contextual information to support the points they were trying to make.
70422k-jun24-02-q: This question, on the increase in international tension, was the most popular on the paper and the most successful in achieving the highest levels. A feature of the good answers was a secure knowledge of the Naval laws, Wilhelm’s foreign policy, and the Imperial superiority of Britain. There was an impressive awareness of the actions of Russia and France as balance. Weaker answers were able to show an awareness of the issues but lacked the precision of detail to explain the impact as well as some very one- sided answers that disregarded Britain at all as a cause for the rise in tensions. The Fashoda incident was downplayed too swiftly by a number of students leading to unbalanced answers where this was their only fact supporting Britain as responsible. A key to unlocking this explanation was the recognition of the phrase ‘responsible’, which led to an examination of cause and consequence. There was some very good knowledge of the Naval race and alliance systems that were put in place in and around this period although some answers drifted way beyond the time parameters and therefore couldn’t be credited.
70422k-jun24-03-q: The topic ‘Crises in the Balkans’ was the least popular essay option. There were different ways to successfully address this question, but there were too many answers that were unbalanced and simply dismissed any notion that the Great Powers dealt effectively with any of the issues presented in the time frame. The vast majority of students were aware of, and could support with some detail, the first and second Balkan wars but there was a number of answers that failed to go beyond this which led to a lack of range across the time period. More successful answers demonstrated knowledge of Russia’s stance in the Bosnian Crisis of 1908 and took an overview approach that the Great Powers managed to contain the Crises in the Balkans in 1913. There was less knowledge about the decline of Turkey, or Austria’s actions in the Treaty of London (1913), although these were features of very strong answers which convincingly explained why the Great Powers failed to deal with the issue of rising nationalism in the region. Any answer which gave a good balanced assessment of the impact of Treaty of London was credited as such and some answers developed a nuanced approach whereby they explained how some of the Great Powers did one thing whilst other Great Powers undermined them.
70422k-jun24-04-q:
The focus of this question on the view that the League of Nations was weakened by the absence of the USA presented a number of challenges. The weaker responses were characterised by a lack of specific context within the date period specified, or by the failure to balance the answer by using counter factual history to support their points. A number of answers started with long narratives of the Paris Peace Settlement and Wilson’s 14 points or strayed at length past 1923 including events such as Manchuria (1931). However, there were a number of good answers. The most analytical were able to distinguish between the effects of the absence of the USA and the decision making of those who were in the League such as Britain and France. Stronger answers were able to balance their responses with good knowledge of the absence of Germany and Russia from the league in this period. What was required was a balanced assessment and many students used some of the successes the league had (such as the Aaland Islands) to suggest that the League was not weakened in this period due to the absence of the USA and these

answers were duly credited. The students were secure on the issues such as Poland, the Washington Conference and the Ruhr but less so on the Corfu incident. There was quite good knowledge of the league being seen as a “Winners’ Club” and a “Lame Duck” but any reference to events outside the given years could only be credited only as far as they were used to enhance the argument offered about 1919-1923 which were few and far between.
70422k-jun25-01-q:
With this question, students were required to evaluate the value of three separate sources in relation to the July Crisis in 1914. They were not asked to compare the given sources and those who did wasted valuable time, although they were not penalised for so doing. The answer did not require an introduction or an overall conclusion, but some concluding judgement on each source in relation to the question posed was helpful to meet the criteria for the highest marks. The best answers were a nuanced evaluation of both provenance and content of the sources. Formulaic, rote-learned approaches were often less effective. A significant number of students were able to identify features about provenance but then were not able to evaluate this beyond a simple comment such as ‘they were there at the time and so this source is accurate’. This approach often leads to much speculation around provenance (for example assuming that the Manchester Guardian gave the views of Britain as a whole or that diary entries must be truthful) which is not then borne out by the content of the source. The best answers were able to combine the two. Simply identifying provenance and making a vague assertion about tone does not lead to higher marks.

There were a persistent minority making very few references to ‘value’ at all and conflating this with validity, utility, reliability and accuracy, which are not the same thing. There were still a number of students paraphrasing the sources and offering very little if any contextual information to support the points they were trying to make.

Source A: Many responses included generalised comments about the nature of diaries, such as their perceived honesty or privacy, without deeper critical engagement. However, content analysis for this source was generally strong, with widespread understanding of the 'Blank Cheque' and Germany’s support for Austria-Hungary.

Source B: There was better handling of the provenance here, though a number of students misidentified the sender, attributing the message to Nicholas. This misreading significantly altered the interpretation of the source. Stronger responses accurately identified Wilhelm’s role and linked the content and provenance to the broader context of the July Crisis, offering limitations where appropriate.

Source C: Many students relied on generic observations about newspapers without adequately situating the source within the context of the July Crisis. Additionally, some responses extended beyond the scope of the question, discussing the broader causes of the First World War. The most effective answers focused specifically on the July Crisis and the aftermath, including the mobilisation of various nations in Europe as well as showing an understanding of the Alliance systems.
70422k-jun25-02-q: This question required an analysis of the causes of the Bosnian Crisis in 1908/9. Stronger responses demonstrated depth of knowledge, addressing the roles of Austria-Hungary, Russia, Serbia and the decline of the Ottoman Empire. Less successful responses often lacked sufficient detail or presented a basic chronological narrative. A few students also diverged from the question by focusing on the consequences of the Ottoman Empire’s collapse rather than its causal role in the crisis. A number of students also gave evidence from way beyond the relevant date range. Some students omitted balance from their answer completely and only focussed on the role of Russia in causing the crisis, therefore limiting their answer.
70422k-jun25-03-q: This question assessed understanding of the 'Spirit of Locarno' during the interwar period. It was essential to adhere to the specified date range, yet several responses included events such as the Corfu or the Aaland Islands Incidents, which fell outside the timeframe and thus weakened the analysis of the specific question. Stronger responses presented well-supported arguments, recognising both the efforts to uphold the spirit of Locarno and the challenges posed by national self-interest. Many also correctly identified the impact of the Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression as key factors that undermined international cooperation. Some responses lacked depth due to the absence of specific examples of international agreements or conferences.
70422k-jun25-04-q: This was the most frequently chosen essay question and produced a number of high-quality responses. The most successful answers were analytical, moving beyond a simple chronological account of Hitler’s actions. Most students were able to identify how Hitler’s foreign policy challenged the Treaty of Versailles and many also explored other aims such as anti-communism (e.g., involvement in the Spanish Civil War or the Anti-Comintern Pact), the pursuit of Lebensraum and the signing of the Nazi-Soviet Pact in 1939, and made judgements based on the evidence given. Less successful responses tended to be more descriptive and lacked the depth required for higher-level analysis and substantiated judgements.
70422l-jun22-01-q:
The sources were on the issue of education in Fascist Italy in the 1930s. The majority of students got off to a good start with source A. Perhaps they were already familiar with sources of this type. Nearly all were able to recognise this as an example of education used as propaganda, although the better answers used their knowledge of the context alongside the provenance of the source to show exactly how it was propaganda. A weakness in some answers was to focus their answer more on the nature of the March on Rome than the topic of education. A feature of very good assessments of this source was the number of points of value that could be drawn, from the age of the children, the subject matter and the role of education to support wider social rituals. It was also recognised that the source represented an ‘ideal’ lesson promoted by the Fascist state, and not necessarily what went on in the classroom.

Source B was understood, particularly in the idea that teachers would ‘go along’ with the regime for their own reasons rather than through a commitment to Fascism. Some weaker answers overlooked the provenance detail about the political background of the author. Those that recognised this and suggested that it might be ‘exaggerated’ were not always able to challenge the source content from their contextual understanding. Good answers recognised the critical tone adopted by Finer, particularly the reference to being ‘netted’, or ‘’caught outside’ in line 12. Relevant contextual knowledge used in answers on this source included the Fascist Teacher Associations and the oath of loyalty.

Source C proved the more difficult for the students to assess. Successful points were made about the respective roles of boys and girls in education and Fascist society, and the importance of physical and military training. Good answers did take note of the date of this charter and made successful links to the radicalisation of society in the later 1930s and the impending military situation. This gave material with which to assess the weaknesses of this source, as it reflected what the state wanted rather than what Italian children were experiencing. It was relevant, in this context, to mention the battle for births and the university ambitions of women. Occasionally the answers strayed into a discussion of social issues and lost the focus on education.

A large majority of students were able to address this question with success. They were able to draw information from each source and say why the provenance of the source, supported by contextual understanding, made this information valuable. Those that could go further, for example by giving a balanced assessment of the sources in regard to value and possible limitations, or to make inferences or draw deductions from the sources, were rewarded with the higher levels.
70422l-jun22-02-q:
This was the least popular question, but only by a narrow margin. Students showed a good knowledge of the economic situation of Italy in 1900, and supporting material was accepted from the period up to 1914. This was balanced with good awareness of other issues, especially the

north-south divided, the political instability and the religious divisions. Balance was also achieved in some cases by the argument that many of Italy’s economic weaknesses, whilst they were acknowledged as significant, were being dealt with through economic development in the north. Better answers related their knowledge of the economy explicitly to the issue of ‘a weakness’ rather than just offering a description of problems facing the economy. This analytical approach was at its strongest when it made links between different aspects of Italian society and political life in an attempt to establish a hierarchy of significance. The economy was most frequently linked to the problems of the north-south divide and the political weaknesses of trasformismo.
70422l-jun22-03-q: This was the most popular question. The consolidation of power is a very popular topic and the period 1922-1926 is well known for the most part. Some weaker answer did have a poor focus on the time period, however. The challenge of this question, which was met by many students, was to identify the specific compromises made by Mussolini and to explain their impacts. The most frequently identified ‘compromises’ were the appointment of de Stefani, the tax policies towards big business, the acceptance of the monarchy and the policies towards the Roman Catholic Church. There is a lot of enthusiasm for writing about Mussolini’s use of violence, and other balancing factors offered were the legality of the laws passed and the weakness of the opposition. A feature of the very strongest answers was the understanding shown of the links between these issues, which included the argument that another of Mussolini’s compromises was the limitations he imposed on the Fascist radicals and Fascist violence.
70422l-jun22-04-q: The given factor of military failures in 1940-1943 proved the more difficult for the students to support and this question was the least successfully answered. Even so, this was marginal and there were some very good answers at the top end. A common weakness of the answers was to give only cursory attention to the military campaigns and a failure to link these to the issue of support for Mussolini in Italy. As balancing factors, the economy and the impact of rationing was well known, as was the lack of support for the war in 1940. Mussolini’s leadership during the war and the failure of wartime propaganda was less well covered, for example the absence of Mussolini from public view due to illness. The strongest answers demonstrated a secure knowledge of the chronology of the war and drew links between the experience of war abroad and the domestic situation, particularly as it reached the crisis of 1943.
70422l-jun23-01-q:
The source selection reflected the issue in the specification ‘Caporetto; the impact of war and defeat on the Home Front’. The sources were understood by the students, with source B perhaps being the trickier because of its predictive nature. Source A captured the imagination of the students, although some went into great length to explain the imagery and construction. A very common response was to agree with Soffici that the soldiers were the victims, with some context about their peasant background and war experience, and also that the government was responsible, with the context of trasformismo, and the changes of government. It was also common to recognise that Soffici might be biased because he was a soldier – he would not blame the soldiers, or because he was a Nationalist – he would be against the government. However, a weakness of these answers was that this analysis often went no further. The source was not challenged and the possible purposes of Soffici in writing, and publishing, were not considered. Therefore, the assessment of value remained rather one-sided. Good and very good answers identified a possible motivation behind the source and related this to the value of the source. It showed the impact of Caporetto on the criticism of the government in the years to come, a theme that was central to source B.

Many students were able to make a link between Source B and the rise in radical politics in 1919. Weaker answers thought that Mussolini was already a Fascist, stronger answers knew that he was in a process of transition and good answers recognised that the elements of Fascist movement might be evident in the phrase ‘class and nation’. It was more common for the word ‘class’ to be prominent in the students’ minds which led to comments on the rise of socialism, which was relevant. Weaker answers commented generally on newspapers as sources for historians, or took the source literally in terms of the conditions at the front. Students with a stronger contextual understanding related the experience of the soldiers in the trenches to their eventual support for the Fascist squads. Again, the successful identification of the purpose of the author, which involved a combination of provenance, content and context, usually made for a very effective assessment of the value of the source.

Source C was accessible. Students knew who Giolitti was and could understand what he was arguing. There were some general and rather unhelpful comments on ‘memoirs’ as a source. It should be emphasised that the attribution is given to be read alongside the content of the source. Better answers pointed out their lack of surprise that Giolitti thought everything got better after he returned, and argued that the piece was a one of self-promotion. There was knowledge about the changes made in the last year of the war and of the debate about the significance of the victory at Vittorio Veneto. Many knew about this victory and offered this as evidence that the source was valuable. There were very strong answers which commented on the significance of the publication being in 1923, at a time when they knew that Giolitti was supporting Mussolini. Those with less secure context thought Giolitti might have been subject to Fascist censorship.

All students respond to the source question at length. The best answers recognise that this question is also about their historical knowledge. Historical context should be used to assess the provenance as well as the content of the source, for example by identifying the purpose of the source. The stronger answers link the assessment of provenance to the content, for example by locating bias in the actual text. Stronger answers use contextual knowledge to both support and challenge the sources, where appropriate.
70422l-jun23-02-q:
This was the most popular question. The establishment of the regime is a popular topic and this question gave the students the opportunity to reflect on the period from the March on Rome to the Lateran Treaty and the election of 1929. The key to a successful answer was the identification of the appeal of Fascist ideology and the linking of that to significant groups or events. Students showed good knowledge of nationalism and Mussolini’s promise to make Italy a great nation, which they linked to the early foreign policy successes. They were also confident on the Cult of the Duce and the importance of the relationship with the Catholic Church. There was also a good understanding that Fascist ideology was a flexible thing. Issues such as anti-Socialism and Corporatism were used as alternate factors in the main, violence for the former, and defeat of the opposition, trade unions, for the latter.

It was commonly argued that Mussolini made allies with big business by cutting taxes, but references to de Stefani tended to overlook the fact that he was not a Fascist and was not following ‘Fascist’ economic policies. Credit was given to references to OND and ONB where they could argue that it had an impact on the regime in the 1920s, though in such responses the time frame began to be lost. The stronger answers identified the change to be explained, showing clear knowledge of the situation in 1922 and 1929, and handled the main factor and at least one alternate factor with analysis and precise support. Weaker answers were drawn into narrative

accounts, particularly of Fascist violence. There is good knowledge of the legal changes that were ultimately made. The view persists that Mussolini himself ‘passed the Acerbo Law’, some seeing this, mistakenly, as the use of decree powers.
70422l-jun23-03-q:
The question gave students the opportunity to write about Mussolini’s foreign policy aims, his role as a ‘statesman’ and the early part of the ‘slide towards war’ (to 1938). Most students understood what this question was looking for and were able to offer some balance. The weaker answers were characterised by lack of detail, a vagueness about the time period, and a lack of focus on Europe. Abyssinia proved to be an irresistible temptation to many, who adapted the question to one of ‘commitment to peace’. However, there were many very good responses that used Abyssinia as a turning point in their answer and successfully explained how it impacted directly on Mussolini’s attitudes and actions in Europe.

There was some evidence of a limited understanding of Mussolini’s role at the Munich Conference, which potentially could be used on either side of the argument in this essay. Common errors were bringing the Pact of Steel and the invasion of Albania forward by a year. The strongest answers showed their understanding with a clear overview of Mussolini’s aims and intentions. Various interpretations were presented, including one of periodisation; that everything changed after Abyssinia. Another argument was for underlying consistency of aim, that Mussolini was pursuing Italy’s best interests in changing circumstances.
70422l-jun23-04-q:
This question focused on the final collapse of Fascism in the years 1943 to 1945 and put forward the ‘weaknesses of Salo’ as the given factor. Students had to be able to offer some view and support on the weaknesses of Salo, as merely dismissing it as not important did not convince. A number of very strong answers were seen and this question received the highest percentage of Level 5 marks. Most students were aware that Salo was essentially a puppet state of the Germany, and of its geographical limitations and loss of support. Stronger answers were also aware of the radical policies Mussolini introduced, his loss of key personnel and his poor health. It was argued that where the Fascists had some strength, in the Black Brigades, their brutality caused more opposition.

The argument was balanced, most commonly, with the role of the partisans in the Italian civil war, the advance of the allies and the collapse of the German war effort. Good answers also commented on the position of Italy in 1943 and how Mussolini’s position was weakened by the actions of the Fascist Grand Council after the fall of Sicily. It was relevant to comment on Italy’s war effort to explain this situation, but answers which went back into the 1930s, in seeking the explanation for the final collapse of Fascism were losing focus. A good argument made was that the execution of Mussolini and the circumstances of his public humiliation showed how the failure of Salo finally destroyed the last vestiges of the Mussolini cult.
70422l-jun24-01-q:
The sources were on the issue of ‘the Corporate State in Italy’, with a focus on the use of the corporations to involve or control the workers in the Fascist state, as well as more general references to the provision of welfare, the management of the economy, and the degree of worker support for Fascism. The sources were chosen to reflect a variety of provenances.

Source A was successful as an opening source. Students have become familiar with the nature of Fascist propaganda, and many were able to detect the purpose of Mussolini in making this speech. The wider context of the collapse of the ‘capitalist economy’ was recognised by many as a reference to the Wall Street Crash. The most successful answers challenged the claims that Mussolini was making, even pointing out that the Corporate State dated from 1925-1926 and so this linking to 1929 could be a relaunch. This was seen as evidence that the Corporate State had failed in Italy. Less successful answers

tended to take information from the source, about the founding of the corporations and the role of the workers, without effectively challenging the claims that Mussolini was making. In such cases the provenance of the source was commented on but not developed. The last line of the source, which makes the claim that ‘the mass of the Italian workers has come to support the Fascist Revolution’, could have been subject to more scrutiny.

Source B was recognised as a contrasting judgement from a critic of fascism. Students were ready to agree with many of the points made by Togliatti and commented on the context in which the lecture was made, which was regarded as a weakness of the source. There was some recognition of why Communists were interested in the fate of the workers in Italy and why they were in exile. More successful answers were able to challenge the claims of the source, suggesting that the achievements of the Corporate State were being overlooked, for example the protection of the workers from some of the effects of the Great Depression.

Source C was seen as valuable for giving an independent perspective, from a journalist who was able to make comparative comments. It was the most balanced of the sources. Those with good or very good contextual knowledge were able to support the judgement that the workers had lost the most under the Corporate State. There were thoughtful comments on Gunther’s claim that Mussolini had propped up the capitalist structure, though not by intention. Wider context was sometimes deployed to reflect on Mussolini’s relationship with the industrial elites. The content of this source was supported with reference to the fall in real wages in the 1930s.
70422l-jun24-02-q: The question gave the students a framework for a balanced assessment of Italy in the decade before the First World War. Knowledge of the policy of ‘trasformismo’ is quite secure, although there is less acknowledgement of the electoral management that this involved. There is a misapprehension that there were established political parties such as the PPI in Italy in this period. Giolitti was recognised as a stable political element, with reference to the breadth of support for his social reforms. The consequences of the Libyan War, the extension of the franchise, and of the Gentolini pact in 1913 were deployed to suggest political instability. The economic situation of Italy was familiar, particularly the continuing north-south divide. Less successful answers showed an awareness of the issues of the period but lacked a secure chronology.
70422l-jun24-03-q: ‘Fascist opposition to Socialism’ proved to be a very successful route into an analysis of Mussolini’s rise to power. Good use was made of the time period, up to and including the March on Rome. The role of violence was recognised, and the importance of the contrast with the apparent ineffectiveness of the Liberal government. This was seen as helping the Fascists to build a relationship with the elites, and the support the Fascist received in the years to 1922 was acknowledged. Strong answers also commented in the importance of ideology, and the changes made by Mussolini to make Fascism more acceptable for government. Balancing factors included the weakness of the Liberal government, the mutilated victory and the economic problems after the war. The strongest responses saw links between the factors. Students are to be reminded that, in questions such as these, the ‘given factor’ must have some consideration. It is usually more successful to do this before ‘other factors’ are introduced, as this enables links to be identified and explored.
70422l-jun24-04-q:
This question focused on the consequences of the Abyssinian War in the period 1935 to 1939. The content of this period is familiar. The question enabled students to deal with ‘Mussolini and Italy’ as a single entity, or to distinguish between them as a means of analysis. Either approach was effective. The stronger answers offered an analytical framework by setting out a clear argument at the outset. The distinction between short- and long-term consequences was used, as was the overall view that the Abyssinian War represented a ‘turning point’ for Mussolini. The consequences were explored both domestically and in international affairs and good use was made of the period to 1939.

The answers showed good knowledge of the propaganda value of the war, the role of ideology, and the fulfilment of colonial ambitions. The negative economic consequences of the war are well known. Whilst some answers described events after 1935 with only a cursory examination of the link with Abyssinia, stronger responses explained the consequential ties, for example the economic and diplomatic dependence on Germany. There were good comments on the links to the radicalisation of the regime in the later 1930s.
70422l-jun25-01-q:
The sources defined the issue, as they all dated from Italy circa 1930, and this coincides with a period when the Fascist regime appeared to be successful and widely supported. A wide range of content was deployed, and this was credited if it supported the points made in the source. The order in which the students deal with the three aspects of this question (source content, context and provenance) varies but it is important that the three elements are brought together in the judgement and not treated separately.

Source A was an accessible opening source and successful in assessment. The arguments made, that the Lateran Treaty had influenced the support for Fascism, and that Fascism was uniting the nation, were recognised and subject to scrutiny from contextual knowledge. The more successful answers recognised that there was a superficiality to some of the comments

made by Cicely Hamilton, which she partly acknowledges herself. Good understanding of the provenance enabled these answers to link the authorship to the judgements made, thereby giving a balanced response. Such answers accessed Levels 4 and 5. Less successful answers tended to either only support the source, or sometimes challenge it, and failed to comment meaningfully on the provenance to reinforce these comments. Students should be encouraged to do more than rewrite the provenance given in the exam paper, and should avoid ‘stock’ evaluations of provenance, such as that ‘journalists make up stories to sensationalise’. More perceptive students could see that, although the source was written and published in Britain, it was very possible that the author had been influenced by Fascist propaganda.

Source B proved to be the most challenging source of the three. The provenance called for a little more reflection. Less successful answers assumed that Gentile, being a Fascist, would be ‘biased’. Often this was not further elaborated on, but sometimes it was assumed that Gentile would favour the Fascists, would not be critical, and would exaggerate the levels of support. The source content suggests the opposite. More successful responses recognised that this was a statement from the heart of the regime, recognising the limits of Fascist support. It was argued that Gentile’s view of what constituted support for Fascism was extreme. There was good understanding across many answers that Italians supported Fascism for a variety of reasons, and context from later in the 1930s was also deployed to show that Gentile was not successful in instilling ‘iron military discipline’.

Source C provoked interesting and varied responses. As in the other sources, those who made their mind up rather too quickly about the source provenance were the less successful. For example, deciding that Lajolo became a Partisan and so would be against the Fascists and therefore unreliable. Knowledge of education in Fascist Italy is secure, and the role of teachers in promulgating Fascist ideas well understood. More successful answers interrogated the source more thoroughly, recognising that the influence of Fascism was felt throughout society, and that there appeared to be no effective opposition which could reach Lajolo. Successful answers also commented thoughtfully on the tone of the piece, reflecting on the feelings of the writer when looking back, and found the descriptions of life in Northern Italy to be authentic, even remorseful. Provenance was successfully used to comment on the temporary nature of Fascist support, and on the possibility that the North of Italy was not necessarily representative, with supporting context.
70422l-jun25-02-q:
The focus of this question was the consequences of the Libyan war on Italy in the years 1911 to 1914. The contention that the war weakened Italy was widely understood, but there was some variance in the focus of the counterarguments deployed. The most successful were able to explain a trail of consequences arising from the war, which encompassed economic problems and political stability, including the rise of the Nationalists and the challenge of the Socialist party. Balanced comment on this included the recognition that Italy had achieved a colony and that, in the short-term at least, the war was widely supported. There is a concentration of focus on the weaknesses of Italy in the years to 1914. An alternate counterargument was offered that the weaknesses of 1911-1914 were wider than the Libyan war. These responses were credited if they maintained the focus on the period. Less successful answers gave a more general commentary on the problems of Italy before the First

World War. More successful answers showed understanding of a wide range of consequences of the war, including its international impact and effect on the decision of Italy not to intervene in the First World War in 1914.
70422l-jun25-03-q: The focus of the question was the appointment of Mussolini as prime minister. The question referred specifically to the year 1922. Whilst there were long term reasons for the rise of Fascism, it was not inevitable that Mussolini would become prime minister in 1922, and the strongest answers showed a depth of knowledge about the circumstances which had made Mussolini an acceptable candidate for the King, including the March on Rome. Context from earlier years could be used to illustrate the issues but, to be rewarded as specific and precise support, such knowledge needed to be explicitly linked to the situation in 1922. Answers which showed an awareness of the issues, but drew on context from more distant periods, for example with detailed description of the impact of the First World War, tended to be less successful.
